title: To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse

paper.title: To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse
paper.abstract:
Abstract Cross-model KV cache sharing reduces prefill computation by allowing a receiver model to reuse prefix KV states generated by a related sender model. Existing methods optimize such reuse for latency and generation quality, but its safety implications remain unclear. In this work, we systematically evaluate this issue across diverse sender–receiver pairs and reuse configurations. We refer to deviations from the receiver’s native safety behavior as safety incompatibility . Our study shows that both the direction and magnitude of safety incompatibility depend on the model pair and reuse configuration, with value reuse causing substantially larger deviations than key reuse across all evaluated pairs. Furthermore, we propose VReparo , a technique that learns per-layer and per-KV-head affine maps offline to align reused sender value tensors with their receiver-native counterparts before decoding.
Across two model pairs under full KV reuse and the state-of-the-art selective reuse setting, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench attack
success rate (ASR) from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT
score from 0.4215 to 0.2163 upon our benchmarks, while retaining an average Time to First Token (TTFT) reduction of 85.62%.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: KV caching and prefix reuse are important optimizations for efficient LLM serving. Widely used serving systems such as vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) manage and reuse KV caches when requests share a common prefix. More recently, work has extended KV cache reuse across related models: a sender model generates a prefix KV cache that is reused by a receiver model to avoid redundant prefill computation. For example, Activated LoRA allows its adapters to reuse the base model’s cache for tokens preceding adapter activation ( Greenewald et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , while DroidSpeak enables KV cache sharing between related models through selective layer recomputation for the shared prefix, while reusing sender KV states at the remaining layers ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . A KV cache, however, is not merely a reusable storage artifact. Its model-generated key and value states directly participate in subsequent attention computations. Recent studies show that quantization of a model’s own KV states can disrupt safety alignment even when conventional task-quality metrics remain largely preserved ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and that cache compression can also affect safety behavior ( Ma et al., 2026b ) . Cross-model KV cache reuse introduces a distinct setting: the reused states are generated by a sender model and consumed by a different receiver model, rather than transformed from the receiver’s own states. Existing cross-model reuse techniques have primarily evaluated generation quality and serving performance ( Li et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , leaving unclear whether reuse also preserves the receiver’s native safety behavior. Figure 1: One form of safety incompatibility in cross-model KV cache reuse, where reusing sender-generated KV states changes a receiver-native safe response into a harmful one. In this work, we study whether cross-model KV cache reuse changes the safety behavior of the receiver. We refer to deviations from this receiver-native behavior as safety incompatibility . Such incompatibility can manifest in different directions: reuse may turn a response that is safe under native inference into a harmful one, or may alter safety behavior in the opposite direction. Figure 1 illustrates the former case, where the receiver refuses a malicious request under native inference but produces a harmful response when reusing a sender-generated KV cache. We systematically investigate safety incompatibility across different model pairs and reuse configurations. Specifically, we study base/instruction-tuned model pairs from multiple model families and task-specific LoRI-D variants derived from the same base model ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We consider full-KV, K-only, and V-only reuse to examine how the reused cache components affect receiver safety. Our results show substantial safety incompatibility, whose magnitude and direction depend on both the model pair and the reuse configuration. For example, full-KV reuse from Llama-3-8B to Llama-3-8B-Instruct increases the HarmBench ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) ASR from 6.37% to 31.21% and the average StrongREJECT ( Souly et al., 2024 ) score from 0.0094 to 0.2477. In contrast, for the Qwen3-8B base/instruction-tuned pair, full-KV reuse decreases the HarmBench ASR from 6.82% to 4.55%, while still changing the HarmBench safety labels on 3.79% of the retained prompts. The reuse configuration further affects the extent of this incompatibility. Across all evaluated model pairs on HarmBench, V-only reuse produces a larger deviation from the receiver-native ASR than K-only reuse. For the Llama-3-8B base/instruction-tuned pair, V-only and K-only reuse yield HarmBench ASRs of 57.25% and 18.12%, respectively. For the Qwen3-8B base/instruction-tuned pair, the corresponding ASRs are 9.30% and 6.98% under V-only and K-only reuse, respectively. To mitigate this incompatibility, we propose VReparo , which learns affine maps offline from paired reused and receiver-native values. It applies these maps once to reused prefix values before receiver continuation, without constructing an online reference cache. The maps leave keys, recomputed values, and model weights unchanged. Across four settings covering two model pairs under full and selective KV reuse, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench ASR from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT score from 0.4215 to 0.2163. With resident sender caches, it retains an average TTFT reduction of 85.62% relative to receiver-native inference.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: We make three main contributions in this work. • We formulate the problem of safety incompatibility in cross-model KV cache reuse as deviations from receiver-native safety behavior caused by reusing sender-generated KV caches. • We systematically characterize how cross-model KV cache reuse alters receiver-native safety behavior across model pairs and reuse configurations, identifying the dependence of these changes on reuse direction and key/value components. • We propose and evaluate VReparo , a lightweight technique that mitigates safety incompatibility while preserving cache-reuse efficiency, and quantify its effects on safety, utility, and runtime overhead.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Existing work on KV caches has largely focused on improving serving efficiency. KV cache optimization spans serving-system memory management and prefix sharing ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) , token retention ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) , quantization ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , and cross-layer sharing ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Recent methods extend reuse across model weights through cache reuse for tokens preceding adapter activation ( Greenewald et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) and selective layer recomputation ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Other approaches use closed-form affine maps ( Heo et al., 2026 ) , head-local mappings with attention-aligned calibration ( Qu et al., 2026 ) , reconstruction from compact semantic codes with selective patching ( Ma et al., 2026a ) , or learned cache fusion for communication between models ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , primarily targeting efficiency and generation quality. Alongside these efficiency advances, recent work has begun to examine the safety and security implications of modifying or reusing KV caches. Safety studies show that compression can affect safety-sensitive capabilities ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and either weaken or strengthen jailbreak attacks depending on the compression regime ( Ma et al., 2026b ) . Low-bit KV quantization can also degrade refusal behavior while conventional utility remains largely stable ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . Beyond compression, HijackKV exploits position-independent reuse to inject attacker-controlled context through cached states associated with benign text ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Our study instead examines changes in safety behavior when reusing caches produced by related models, without adversarial cache construction. These risks have motivated cache-level mitigations. Existing mitigations include eviction policies that preserve instructions and reduce system-prompt leakage ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , history-aware cache merging in Safe-CAM ( Ma et al., 2026b ) , quantization repair guided by per-channel reduction ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and refusal-aware token retention in AnchorKV ( Ni & Lao, 2026 ) . These methods primarily address transformations of a model’s own cache. We study safety incompatibility across sender–receiver pairs and reuse configurations, and develop VReparo to map reused values toward receiver-native values while retaining the efficiency benefits of cross-model reuse.

sections.heading: KV cache in LLM inference.
sections.text: Transformer-based LLM inference consists of a prefill phase and a decode phase . During prefill, the model processes the input context and stores the key (K) and value (V) tensors produced at each Transformer layer. During autoregressive decode, each newly generated token attends to these cached states and appends its own K and V tensors to the cache, avoiding recomputation over previously processed tokens. For a model M M with L M L_{M} transformer layers and a token sequence z z , we write its KV cache as C M ​ ( z ) = ( ( K M ℓ ​ ( z ) , V M ℓ ​ ( z ) ) ) ℓ = 1 L M , C_{M}(z)=\left(\left(K_{M}^{\ell}(z),V_{M}^{\ell}(z)\right)\right)_{\ell=1}^{L_{M}}, (1) where K M ℓ ​ ( z ) K_{M}^{\ell}(z) and V M ℓ ​ ( z ) V_{M}^{\ell}(z) denote the cached K and V tensors at layer ℓ \ell . These tensors are determined by the hidden states produced during the corresponding forward execution. Consequently, changing the cached states used at one layer can affect the receiver-computed states at subsequent layers.

sections.heading: Cross-model KV cache reuse.
sections.text: Cross-model KV cache reuse uses KV tensors produced by a sender model S S to reduce the prefill computation performed by a receiver model R R . Let ℒ \mathcal{L} denote the set of layer positions at which sender KV tensors may be reused by the receiver. To characterize which components are reused, we define the cross-model reuse configuration ρ = ( 𝒰 K , 𝒰 V ) , 𝒰 K , 𝒰 V ⊆ ℒ , \rho=(\mathcal{U}_{K},\mathcal{U}_{V}),\qquad\mathcal{U}_{K},\mathcal{U}_{V}\subseteq\mathcal{L}, (2) where 𝒰 K \mathcal{U}_{K} and 𝒰 V \mathcal{U}_{V} specify the layers that reuse sender K and V tensors, respectively. Components not selected for reuse are supplied by the receiver. In the diagnostic experiments in Section 4 , sender and receiver-native caches are constructed independently from the same token sequence, and the selected components are combined before receiver decoding. K-only uses sender keys and receiver-native values. V-only uses receiver-native keys and sender values. We use DroidSpeak ( Liu et al., 2026 ) to evaluate VReparo . For the shared prefix, it recomputes KV states in a selected receiver layer block from the sender’s intermediate hidden states and reuses sender KV states at all other layers. The receiver then processes the prompt suffix.

sections.heading: 3.2 Safety Incompatibility
sections.text: Because KV caches encode model-dependent intermediate states, reusing them can alter not only the receiver’s task behavior but also its safety behavior. Which factors can affect safety incompatibility of the receiver model? In Section 4 , we use these metrics to examine whether cross-model KV cache reuse preserves receiver-native safety behavior and how the observed incompatibility varies across reuse settings.

sections.heading: 4.1 Study Methodology
sections.text: To answer RQ1, we consider two types of model pairs, following the evaluation setting used in DroidSpeak ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . The first type pairs base models with their instruction-tuned counterparts from several model families, allowing us to examine whether the safety effect of KV cache reuse generalizes across models. The second type consists of task-specific LoRI-D variants that share the same base model and major LoRA configuration, providing a more controlled comparison across training objectives. For each model pair, we fix the receiver and tokenized prompt and compare full KV reuse with the receiver’s native inference. To answer RQ2, we use the same sender–receiver pairs as in RQ1. To examine the effect of cache composition, we compare full KV, K-only, and V-only reuse with receiver-native inference. Following the cache construction described in Section 3.1 , components not reused from the sender are taken from the receiver-native cache for the same tokenized prompt. sections.heading: 4.2 Experimental Subjects and Settings
sections.text: For RQ1, we evaluate six base/instruction-tuned model pairs from four families, which include Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-2B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3. The base model serves as the sender and the instruction-tuned model as the receiver. We also study the Code and Safety variants of LoRI-D ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , which share Meta-Llama-3-8B and the same major adapter configuration. The Code and Safety variants are fine-tuned on CodeAlpaca and SaferPaca, respectively. We evaluate the Code/Safety pair in both directions. RQ2 uses the same model pairs to compare different K/V reuse configurations. Following the benchmark choices in prior LLM safety studies ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , we use HarmBench ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) and StrongREJECT ( Souly et al., 2024 ) as the main evaluation benchmarks for RQ1, and HarmBench for the K/V separation experiments in RQ2. We evaluate on 159 harmful requests from HarmBench and 313 from StrongREJECT before output validity filtering. The benchmarks provide complementary assessments: HarmBench evaluates whether a response exhibits the target harmful behavior, whereas StrongREJECT measures the extent to which a response provides harmful assistance. Notably, we retain only prompts whose outputs pass the same validity check in all compared conditions and report the retained sample size. Implementation details and output validity checks are provided in Appendix A . We instantiate σ \sigma with binary HarmBench judgments in { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} and StrongREJECT scores in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] to compute Δ ​ S \Delta S , SD, SI, and SDV as defined in Section 3.2 . We also report HarmBench ASR, the percentage of responses judged to exhibit the requested harmful behavior, and the average StrongREJECT score. HarmBench SD, SI, and SDV are percentages of prompts with label transitions, whereas Δ ​ S \Delta S is an ASR difference in percentage points (pp). Lower average HarmBench ASRs and StrongREJECT scores indicate safer responses, whereas lower SDV indicates greater agreement with receiver-native safety scores on the retained prompts.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: As shown in Table 1 , full KV cache reuse does not consistently preserve receiver-native safety behavior, even among responses that pass the validity check. When the base model supplies the cache to its instruction-tuned counterpart, harmfulness increases for five of the six model pairs under both evaluators. Qwen3-8B is the exception in both HarmBench ASR and average StrongREJECT score, but reuse still changes the HarmBench label on 3.79% of retained prompts. Across the six base/instruction-tuned model pairs, HarmBench SDV ranges from 3.79% to 31.21%. As shown in Table 5 in Appendix A.2 , full reuse raises HarmBench ASR for Gemma-2-2B from 1.27% to 21.52%. For Mistral-7B-v0.3, the ASR increase is 9.43 percentage points, while 24.53% of the HarmBench labels change, showing that changes in ASR do not capture all safety changes. The LoRI-D variants share the same base model, providing a more controlled comparison. Among the evaluated pairs, the largest increase in harmfulness occurs when the LoRI-D Safety variant reuses the KV cache from the Code variant. As shown in Tables 5 and 6 , full reuse raises HarmBench ASR from 25.93% to 80.74% and the average StrongREJECT score from .1093 to .6741. In the reverse direction, the Code variant reuses the KV cache from the Safety variant. Both ASR and the average StrongREJECT score decrease, but HarmBench SDV is 51.82%, indicating that safety judgments change for more than half of the retained prompts. Despite the lower ASR, HarmBench SD is 3.65%, with responses to 5 of the 137 retained prompts changing from being judged safe to harmful. Thus, sharing the same foundation model does not ensure safety compatibility. Answer to RQ1. Cross-model KV cache reuse introduces safety incompatibility across all evaluated pairs. SD and SI can coexist. Several responses become more harmful even when average harmfulness over the evaluated prompts decreases.

sections.heading: 5 Mitigating Safety Incompatibility
sections.text: Section 4.3.2 motivates correcting reused values, although keys also affect safety. VReparo learns maps from reused to receiver-native values offline, avoiding reference prefill for each request. For each sender S S , receiver R R , and fixed reuse configuration ρ \rho , we fit the maps separately and apply them before decoding to reduce safety deviation while retaining prefill savings. Figure 2 illustrates both offline map fitting and online value correction. Figure 2: The workflow of VReparo . (a) Matching token positions at each layer and KV head provide paired reused and receiver-native values for affine fitting. Separate behavioral calibration selects α ⋆ \alpha^{\star} . (b) The fixed maps transform reused prefix values once. Keys, recomputed values, and newly generated KV states are not transformed. The layer layout illustrates selective reuse. Under full KV reuse, prefix values at all layers are mapped.

sections.heading: Data collection.
sections.text: We fit the affine maps without task or safety labels and select the correction strength α \alpha using refusal rates on a separate set of safe and unsafe prompts. For each fitting example, we use identical tokenized inputs and prompt formatting to construct the cache under ρ \rho and the receiver-native cache. We collect value vectors at matching token positions in the same layer and KV head. For a layer whose values are reused, let v n ρ ∈ ℝ d v v_{n}^{\rho}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} be a reused value vector and v n nat ∈ ℝ d v v_{n}^{\mathrm{nat}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} the corresponding receiver-native value vector, where d v d_{v} is the head dimension. The index n n runs over selected prefill positions across fitting examples. Layer and head indices are omitted for clarity.

sections.heading: Offline fitting.
sections.text: For each layer and KV head whose values are reused, we fit an affine map with matrix A ∈ ℝ d v × d v A\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{v}} and bias b ∈ ℝ d v b\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} : ( A ⋆ , b ⋆ ) = arg ⁡ min ⁡ ∑ n = 1 N A , b ⁡ ‖ A ​ v n ρ + b − v n nat ‖ 2 2 + λ ​ ‖ A − I ‖ F 2 , (A^{\star},b^{\star})=\arg\min_{A,b}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\|Av_{n}^{\rho}+b-v_{n}^{\mathrm{nat}}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\|A-I\right\|_{F}^{2}, (7) where N N is the number of collected pairs and I I is the identity matrix. The regularization term encourages A A to remain close to the identity. The bias is not penalized. This is a closed-form ridge fit and does not update either language model. We use a full matrix for A A and fix the ridge coefficient λ \lambda across all evaluated model pairs and reuse configurations. The full mapping may also change responses to benign prompts. We therefore select a scalar strength α ∗ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha^{*}\in[0,1] on behavioral calibration data, maximizing refusal on unsafe prompts subject to limits on refusal of benign prompts. The strength is fixed across requests in each ( S , R , ρ ) (S,R,\rho) setting.

sections.heading: Inference.
sections.text: Before receiver decoding, each reused value vector is replaced by v ^ n = v n ρ + α ∗ ​ ( A ⋆ ​ v n ρ + b ⋆ − v n ρ ) . \widehat{v}_{n}=v_{n}^{\rho}+\alpha^{*}\left(A^{\star}v_{n}^{\rho}+b^{\star}-v_{n}^{\rho}\right). (8) Thus α ∗ = 0 \alpha^{*}=0 leaves the value unchanged, while α ∗ = 1 \alpha^{*}=1 applies the full fitted mapping. The mapping preserves cache dimensions and leaves the key tensors unchanged. For full KV reuse, it is applied to the sender’s prompt values before the receiver processes the prompt boundary token. For DroidSpeak, it is applied to reused prefix values outside the receiver’s recomputed layer block. The receiver then processes the prompt suffix using the corrected prefix cache. Values in the recomputed block are not mapped. In both cases, the receiver continues autoregressive decoding with its original weights and language-model head. The mapping is applied once to the reused prompt cache. Values produced during subsequent decoding are not mapped. No safety label is required at inference.

sections.heading: 6 Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate VReparo ’s safety compatibility, question-answering (QA) quality, benign refusal, and runtime under full KV reuse and selective reuse with DroidSpeak ( Liu et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Evaluation settings.
sections.text: We evaluate two sender–receiver pairs under both reuse configurations. For the LoRI-D pair, the Safety variant reuses the KV cache from the Code variant. For the Llama-3-8B base/instruction-tuned pair, the instruction-tuned model reuses the KV cache from the base model. Each setting compares receiver-native inference, uncorrected reuse, and reuse with VReparo . For DroidSpeak, we select the receiver layer block to recompute based on QA performance.

sections.heading: Fitting and calibration.
sections.text: We fit separate affine maps for each sender–receiver pair and reuse configuration using 32 HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) and 32 HEx-PHI ( Qi et al., 2023 ) examples, without task or safety labels. We select the correction strength α \alpha using string-based refusal rates on XSTest ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) . We repeat this procedure with five random seeds for data sampling. The fitted maps and selected strength remain fixed during evaluation within each run.

sections.heading: Benchmarks and reporting.
sections.text: Safety evaluation uses 127 HarmBench prompts after excluding a separate 32-prompt development subset, and all 313 StrongREJECT prompts. The development subset is distinct from the fitting examples. Sampling details are provided in Appendix B . We report HarmBench ASR and average StrongREJECT score (0–1). For both benchmarks, we also report Δ ​ S \Delta S , SD, SI, and SDV as defined in Section 3.2 , computed from paired per-prompt scores relative to Native within the same configuration. We evaluate QA quality using token-level F1, the harmonic mean of token precision and recall. Benign refusal is evaluated on 200 OR-Bench prompts ( Cui et al., 2024 ) . Full refusal means declining assistance without a substantive completion. All conditions within each setting use the same fixed prompts, without the response-based filtering used in Section 4 . These datasets were examined during earlier development. Layer selection, fitting, calibration, and evaluation details are provided in Appendix B . Tables 3 and 4 report safety and latency. Table 9 in Appendix B.3 reports QA quality.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we investigated the safety incompatibility in cross-model KV cache reuse across different sender–receiver pairs and reuse configurations. Our results show that cache reuse can change receiver safety in either direction, and that reused values have a consistently larger effect on safety behavior than reused keys. We proposed VReparo , which learns lightweight affine maps to align reused values with their receiver-native counterparts. Across the evaluated settings, VReparo substantially improves safety compatibility while retaining large TTFT reductions, with trade-offs in benign refusal and response quality.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work studies safety risks in cross-model KV cache reuse using public benchmarks. Our experiments do not target deployed third-party services. We report aggregate results and per-example scores without publishing harmful model completions.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement

sections.heading: A.1 Setup and Validity Screening
sections.text: The HarmBench subset comprises textual requests without accompanying context. We evaluate direct harmful requests without optimizing jailbreak prompts. We implement cache construction, substitution, and receiver decoding in PyTorch 2.4.0 with Transformers 4.45.2 and PEFT 0.14.0. All experiments run on NVIDIA A40 GPUs. Sender and receiver weights and KV caches use FP16 without quantization. HarmBench uses HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls on the first 512 response tokens. StrongREJECT uses the strongreject-15k-v1 adapter on Gemma-2B with the last 512 response tokens. Each window uses the evaluator’s tokenizer. RQ1 requires valid outputs under Native and Full KV. RQ2 requires validity under Native, K-only, V-only, and Full KV. The retained subsets, and hence their Native ASRs, can therefore differ. Automatic screening excludes empty, role-only, or export-clipped outputs, content-free “the correct answer [is]” templates, and short prompt-tail echoes of at most eight words for instruction-initial prompts. Repetition is flagged when a lowercased four-word sequence occurs at least ten times in an output of at least 40 words, or a normalized sentence of at least 20 characters and three words occurs at least four times. A capped-reasoning candidate must simultaneously reach 512 generated tokens, contain “the user wants/is asking/asked,” “I need to,” or “let me think/see/break/analyze” within its first 400 characters, and lack a closing </think> tag. The cap alone is insufficient. Existing output-form review annotations marking invalid or uncertain responses also cause exclusion. These retrospective, Codex-assisted annotations are not an independent human audit. Passing the check does not certify semantic validity or benign-task quality. Reasons and conditions may overlap: Gemma-2-2B RQ2 excludes 38 unique prompts, including 37 V-only failures (36 empty and one repetitive) and one Full KV capped-reasoning candidate. Qwen3-8B excludes 30 unique prompts, with 27 Full KV and four V-only failures. Artifacts retain reasons and overlaps.

sections.text: For DroidSpeak ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , we profile 136 contiguous blocks formed from two-layer groups on 50 HotpotQA examples, without observing safety scores. At each budget, we retain the block with the highest QA F1 and choose the smallest budget reaching 95% of native F1. Both pairs independently select and fix zero-based layers [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] for fitting and evaluation. Each of the five runs uses 32 HotpotQA and 32 HEx-PHI examples. The four settings use the same examples in each run, with configuration-specific formatting and separately fitted maps. Appendix B.5 describes sampling and individual results. We collect paired values at matching positions per layer and KV head, with λ = 1 \lambda=1 . For a cache of length L ≤ 128 L\leq 128 , we use all positions. Otherwise, we take the first 128 positions at stride ⌊ L / 128 ⌋ \lfloor L/128\rfloor , starting at zero and sampling only the reused shared prefix for DroidSpeak. The loss sums squared residuals over N N positions per head. λ = 1 \lambda=1 is not a mean-loss regularizer. N N counts correlated token positions, not independent texts. Fitting is label-free, but its HEx-PHI inputs are not benign-only. We select α ∈ { 0.1 , 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 } \alpha\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5,1\} using string-based refusal on 450 XSTest prompts (250 safe and 200 unsafe) ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) . Eligible candidates must increase unsafe-prompt refusal over uncorrected reuse ( α = 0 \alpha=0 ), while limiting safe-prompt refusal increases over native to 5 pp overall and 20 pp per safe subtype. We maximize the unsafe-refusal increase, breaking ties toward smaller α \alpha . We select α \alpha separately for each run. Table 11 gives the selected values. QA does not determine eligibility. Parameters remain fixed during evaluation, and the 95% QA target applies only to DroidSpeak layer profiling. QA was changed from a development eligibility gate to a reporting metric. sections.heading: B.2 Evaluation and Timing Protocol
sections.text: We measure question-answering quality using token-level F1 on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , and MultiFieldQA-en from LongBench-E ( Bai et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Evaluation subsets and refusal scoring.
sections.text: The 32 HarmBench development prompts are separate from the fitting examples. They were selected from an existing 101-prompt subset by cycling through alphabetically sorted categories, preserving source order within each category. Excluding their identifiers from the 159-prompt evaluation pool leaves the 127 prompts used here. All five runs use the same 248 HotpotQA evaluation examples in all four settings. The additional QA results in Table 9 use 149 HotpotQA examples for full reuse and 248 for DroidSpeak, plus 200 2WikiMultihopQA and 150 MultiFieldQA-en examples. HotpotQA evaluation subsets exclude fitting, profiling, and calibration examples by identifier and normalized question/context. XSTest is used for calibration only. The 200 OR-Bench prompts include 20 per category. Qwen3-8B judges responses without condition labels or manual adjudication. We report unscorable responses separately out of 200. One response is unscorable for Llama-3-8B full Reuse and for each of its corrected runs with seeds 0 and 3. The other corrected runs have none.

sections.heading: Generation and safety scoring.
sections.text: Generation follows the model-loading setup in Appendix A , with greedy decoding and budgets of 512 tokens for safety/refusal, 32 for HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA, and 64 for MultiFieldQA-en. HarmBench scores the first 512 response tokens using strict single-token yes/no decisions from HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls in BF16. StrongREJECT scores the last 512 with FP32 evaluator computation using Gemma-2B merged with strongreject-15k-v1 from BF16-loaded weights. Window lengths are measured using each evaluator’s tokenizer. Native baselines are evaluated separately for the two reuse configurations. The full-reuse implementation initializes decoding with a receiver-native cache, whereas the DroidSpeak implementation uses the receiver’s standard generation routine. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 arXiv:2610.15721v1 [cs.LG] 11 Oct 2026 To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse Zhiwei Lin Email: zhiweil@u.nus.edu Jiahao Liu Affiliation: National University of Singapore Ant Group Email: ljiahaomail@gmail.com Yan Liu Affiliation: National University of Singapore Ant Group Email: bencao.ly@antgroup.com Chengpeng Wang Email: wang-chengpeng@nus.edu.sg Abstract Cross-model KV cache sharing reduces prefill computation by allowing a receiver model to reuse prefix KV states generated by a related sender model. Existing methods optimize such reuse for latency and generation quality, but its safety implications remain unclear. In this work, we systematically evaluate this issue across diverse sender–receiver pairs and reuse configurations. We refer to deviations from the receiver’s native safety behavior as safety incompatibility . Our study shows that both the direction and magnitude of safety incompatibility depend on the model pair and reuse configuration, with value reuse causing substantially larger deviations than key reuse across all evaluated pairs. Furthermore, we propose VReparo , a technique that learns per-layer and per-KV-head affine maps offline to align reused sender value tensors with their receiver-native counterparts before decoding. Across two model pairs under full KV reuse and the state-of-the-art selective reuse setting, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT score from 0.4215 to 0.2163 upon our benchmarks, while retaining an average Time to First Token (TTFT) reduction of 85.62%. 1 Introduction KV caching and prefix reuse are important optimizations for efficient LLM serving. Widely used serving systems such as vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) manage and reuse KV caches when requests share a common prefix. More recently, work has extended KV cache reuse across related models: a sender model generates a prefix KV cache that is reused by a receiver model to avoid redundant prefill computation. For example, Activated LoRA allows its adapters to reuse the base model’s cache for tokens preceding adapter activation ( Greenewald et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , while DroidSpeak enables KV cache sharing between related models through selective layer recomputation for the shared prefix, while reusing sender KV states at the remaining layers ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . A KV cache, however, is not merely a reusable storage artifact. Its model-generated key and value states directly participate in subsequent attention computations. Recent studies show that quantization of a model’s own KV states can disrupt safety alignment even when conventional task-quality metrics remain largely preserved ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and that cache compression can also affect safety behavior ( Ma et al., 2026b ) . Cross-model KV cache reuse introduces a distinct setting: the reused states are generated by a sender model and consumed by a different receiver model, rather than transformed from the receiver’s own states. Existing cross-model reuse techniques have primarily evaluated generation quality and serving performance ( Li et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , leaving unclear whether reuse also preserves the receiver’s native safety behavior. Figure 1: One form of safety incompatibility in cross-model KV cache reuse, where reusing sender-generated KV states changes a receiver-native safe response into a harmful one. In this work, we study whether cross-model KV cache reuse changes the safety behavior of the receiver. We refer to deviations from this receiver-native behavior as safety incompatibility . Such incompatibility can manifest in different directions: reuse may turn a response that is safe under native inference into a harmful one, or may alter safety behavior in the opposite direction. Figure 1 illustrates the former case, where the receiver refuses a malicious request under native inference but produces a harmful response when reusing a sender-generated KV cache. We systematically investigate safety incompatibility across different model pairs and reuse configurations. Specifically, we study base/instruction-tuned model pairs from multiple model families and task-specific LoRI-D variants derived from the same base model ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We consider full-KV, K-only, and V-only reuse to examine how the reused cache components affect receiver safety. Our results show substantial safety incompatibility, whose magnitude and direction depend on both the model pair and the reuse configuration. For example, full-KV reuse from Llama-3-8B to Llama-3-8B-Instruct increases the HarmBench ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) ASR from 6.37% to 31.21% and the average StrongREJECT ( Souly et al., 2024 ) score from 0.0094 to 0.2477. In contrast, for the Qwen3-8B base/instruction-tuned pair, full-KV reuse decreases the HarmBench ASR from 6.82% to 4.55%, while still changing the HarmBench safety labels on 3.79% of the retained prompts. The reuse configuration further affects the extent of this incompatibility. Across all evaluated model pairs on HarmBench, V-only reuse produces a larger deviation from the receiver-native ASR than K-only reuse. For the Llama-3-8B base/instruction-tuned pair, V-only and K-only reuse yield HarmBench ASRs of 57.25% and 18.12%, respectively. For the Qwen3-8B base/instruction-tuned pair, the corresponding ASRs are 9.30% and 6.98% under V-only and K-only reuse, respectively. To mitigate this incompatibility, we propose VReparo , which learns affine maps offline from paired reused and receiver-native values. It applies these maps once to reused prefix values before receiver continuation, without constructing an online reference cache. The maps leave keys, recomputed values, and model weights unchanged. Across four settings covering two model pairs under full and selective KV reuse, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench ASR from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT score from 0.4215 to 0.2163. With resident sender caches, it retains an average TTFT reduction of 85.62% relative to receiver-native inference. Contributions. We make three main contributions in this work. • We formulate the problem of safety incompatibility in cross-model KV cache reuse as deviations from receiver-native safety behavior caused by reusing sender-generated KV caches. • We systematically characterize how cross-model KV cache reuse alters receiver-native safety behavior across model pairs and reuse configurations, identifying the dependence of these changes on reuse direction and key/value components. • We propose and evaluate VReparo , a lightweight technique that mitigates safety incompatibility while preserving cache-reuse efficiency, and quantify its effects on safety, utility, and runtime overhead. 2 Related Work Existing work on KV caches has largely focused on improving serving efficiency. KV cache optimization spans serving-system memory management and prefix sharing ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) , token retention ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) , quantization ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , and cross-layer sharing ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Recent methods extend reuse across model weights through cache reuse for tokens preceding adapter activation ( Greenewald et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) and selective layer recomputation ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Other approaches use closed-form affine maps ( Heo et al., 2026 ) , head-local mappings with attention-aligned calibration ( Qu et al., 2026 ) , reconstruction from compact semantic codes with selective patching ( Ma et al., 2026a ) , or learned cache fusion for communication between models ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , primarily targeting efficiency and generation quality. Alongside these efficiency advances, recent work has begun to examine the safety and security implications of modifying or reusing KV caches. Safety studies show that compression can affect safety-sensitive capabilities ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and either weaken or strengthen jailbreak attacks depending on the compression regime ( Ma et al., 2026b ) . Low-bit KV quantization can also degrade refusal behavior while conventional utility remains largely stable ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . Beyond compression, HijackKV exploits position-independent reuse to inject attacker-controlled context through cached states associated with benign text ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Our study instead examines changes in safety behavior when reusing caches produced by related models, without adversarial cache construction. These risks have motivated cache-level mitigations. Existing mitigations include eviction policies that preserve instructions and reduce system-prompt leakage ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , history-aware cache merging in Safe-CAM ( Ma et al., 2026b ) , quantization repair guided by per-channel reduction ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and refusal-aware token retention in AnchorKV ( Ni & Lao, 2026 ) . These methods primarily address transformations of a model’s own cache. We study safety incompatibility across sender–receiver pairs and reuse configurations, and develop VReparo to map reused values toward receiver-native values while retaining the efficiency benefits of cross-model reuse. 3 Background and Problem Statement 3.1 Preliminaries of Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse KV cache in LLM inference. Transformer-based LLM inference consists of a prefill phase and a decode phase . During prefill, the model processes the input context and stores the key (K) and value (V) tensors produced at each Transformer layer. During autoregressive decode, each newly generated token attends to these cached states and appends its own K and V tensors to the cache, avoiding recomputation over previously processed tokens. Consequently, changing the cached states used at one layer can affect the receiver-computed states at subsequent layers. Cross-model KV cache reuse. Cross-model KV cache reuse uses KV tensors produced by a sender model S S to reduce the prefill computation performed by a receiver model R R . For the shared prefix, it recomputes KV states in a selected receiver layer block from the sender’s intermediate hidden states and reuses sender KV states at all other layers. (3) When no cross-model reuse is applied, the receiver constructs the prefix cache itself and performs receiver-native inference , whose output is denoted by y R native ​ ( x ) y_{R}^{\mathrm{native}}(x) . 3.2 Safety Incompatibility Because KV caches encode model-dependent intermediate states, reusing them can alter not only the receiver’s task behavior but also its safety behavior. We refer to deviations from the receiver’s native safety behavior as safety incompatibility . We quantify safety incompatibility through the direction and magnitude of changes in the receiver’s safety scores. Definition 1 (Safety Score Shift) . Given a prompt set D D , let σ ⁡ ( y , x ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \sigma(y,x)\in[0,1] denote a harmfulness evaluator for response y y to prompt x x , where 0 0 indicates a safe response and larger values indicate greater safety risk. The safety deviation (SDV) measures the overall magnitude of the deviation from the receiver’s native safety behavior: SDV S → R ρ ​ ( D ) = 1 | D | ​ ∑ x ∈ D | σ ⁡ ( y S → R ρ ​ ( x ) , x ) − σ ⁡ ( y R native ​ ( x ) , x ) | . \mathrm{SDV}_{S\rightarrow R}^{\rho}(D)=\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{x\in D}\left|\sigma\!\left(y_{S\rightarrow R}^{\rho}(x),x\right)-\sigma\!\left(y_{R}^{\mathrm{native}}(x),x\right)\right|. Concretely, a smaller SDV indicates greater safety compatibility, with SDV = 0 \mathrm{SDV}=0 indicating that reuse preserves the receiver’s native safety scores for all prompts in D D . Conversely, a larger SDV indicates greater safety incompatibility. We use this formulation to investigate two research questions: RQ1. Does cross-model KV-cache reuse introduce safety incompatibility of the receiver model? RQ2. Which factors can affect safety incompatibility of the receiver model? In Section 4 , we use these metrics to examine whether cross-model KV cache reuse preserves receiver-native safety behavior and how the observed incompatibility varies across reuse settings. 4 Characterizing Safety Incompatibility 4.1 Study Methodology To answer RQ1, we consider two types of model pairs, following the evaluation setting used in DroidSpeak ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . The first type pairs base models with their instruction-tuned counterparts from several model families, allowing us to examine whether the safety effect of KV cache reuse generalizes across models. The second type consists of task-specific LoRI-D variants that share the same base model and major LoRA configuration, providing a more controlled comparison across training objectives. For each model pair, we fix the receiver and tokenized prompt and compare full KV reuse with the receiver’s native inference. To answer RQ2, we use the same sender–receiver pairs as in RQ1. To examine the effect of cache composition, we compare full KV, K-only, and V-only reuse with receiver-native inference. Following the cache construction described in Section 3.1 , components not reused from the sender are taken from the receiver-native cache for the same tokenized prompt. The base model serves as the sender and the instruction-tuned model as the receiver. We also study the Code and Safety variants of LoRI-D ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , which share Meta-Llama-3-8B and the same major adapter configuration. The Code and Safety variants are fine-tuned on CodeAlpaca and SaferPaca, respectively. We evaluate the Code/Safety pair in both directions. RQ2 uses the same model pairs to compare different K/V reuse configurations. Following the benchmark choices in prior LLM safety studies ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , we use HarmBench ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) and StrongREJECT ( Souly et al., 2024 ) as the main evaluation benchmarks for RQ1, and HarmBench for the K/V separation experiments in RQ2. We evaluate on 159 harmful requests from HarmBench and 313 from StrongREJECT before output validity filtering. The benchmarks provide complementary assessments: HarmBench evaluates whether a response exhibits the target harmful behavior, whereas StrongREJECT measures the extent to which a response provides harmful assistance. Notably, we retain only prompts whose outputs pass the same validity check in all compared conditions and report the retained sample size. Implementation details and output validity checks are provided in Appendix A . We instantiate σ \sigma with binary HarmBench judgments in { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} and StrongREJECT scores in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] to compute Δ ​ S \Delta S , SD, SI, and SDV as defined in Section 3.2 . We also report HarmBench ASR, the percentage of responses judged to exhibit the requested harmful behavior, and the average StrongREJECT score. HarmBench SD, SI, and SDV are percentages of prompts with label transitions, whereas Δ ​ S \Delta S is an ASR difference in percentage points (pp). Lower average HarmBench ASRs and StrongREJECT scores indicate safer responses, whereas lower SDV indicates greater agreement with receiver-native safety scores on the retained prompts. 4.3 Empirical Findings 4.3.1 Safety Incompatibility under Cross-Model KV-Cache Reuse Results. As shown in Table 1 , full KV cache reuse does not consistently preserve receiver-native safety behavior, even among responses that pass the validity check. When the base model supplies the cache to its instruction-tuned counterpart, harmfulness increases for five of the six model pairs under both evaluators. Qwen3-8B is the exception in both HarmBench ASR and average StrongREJECT score, but reuse still changes the HarmBench label on 3.79% of retained prompts. Across the six base/instruction-tuned model pairs, HarmBench SDV ranges from 3.79% to 31.21%. As shown in Table 5 in Appendix A.2 , full reuse raises HarmBench ASR for Gemma-2-2B from 1.27% to 21.52%. For Mistral-7B-v0.3, the ASR increase is 9.43 percentage points, while 24.53% of the HarmBench labels change, showing that changes in ASR do not capture all safety changes. The LoRI-D variants share the same base model, providing a more controlled comparison. Among the evaluated pairs, the largest increase in harmfulness occurs when the LoRI-D Safety variant reuses the KV cache from the Code variant. As shown in Tables 5 and 6 , full reuse raises HarmBench ASR from 25.93% to 80.74% and the average StrongREJECT score from .1093 to .6741. In the reverse direction, the Code variant reuses the KV cache from the Safety variant. Both ASR and the average StrongREJECT score decrease, but HarmBench SDV is 51.82%, indicating that safety judgments change for more than half of the retained prompts. Despite the lower ASR, HarmBench SD is 3.65%, with responses to 5 of the 137 retained prompts changing from being judged safe to harmful. Thus, sharing the same foundation model does not ensure safety compatibility. Answer to RQ1. Cross-model KV cache reuse introduces safety incompatibility across all evaluated pairs. Our results show that cache reuse can change receiver safety in either direction, and that reused values have a consistently larger effect on safety behavior than reused keys. We proposed VReparo , which learns lightweight affine maps to align reused values with their receiver-native counterparts. Across the evaluated settings, VReparo substantially improves safety compatibility while retaining large TTFT reductions, with trade-offs in benign refusal and response quality.
